strengths: The paper presents a clear and relevant idea: matching hierarchical fMRI representations to the discrete coarse-to-fine stages of a scale-wise autoregressive image generator. This is a sensible alternative to fixed conditioning in diffusion pipelines.
The hierarchy-to-hierarchy alignment, scale-dependent routing, and autoregressive backbone form a coherent overall framework. The method is technically plausible and reasonably well explained.

Evaluation covers standard NSD subjects and a broad set of low- and high-level reconstruction metrics. The reported semantic results are competitive, including the best CLIP, Inception, EfficientNet, and SwAV results in the non-auxiliary comparison.
The paper includes useful diagnostics on hierarchical supervision, CLIP-layer selection, and inverted guidance order, as well as per-subject and low-data results.
The reported 2.64-second inference time could be practically valuable if confirmed under a controlled hardware and sampling protocol. The qualitative reconstructions are generally convincing.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the method primarily combines a pretrained scale-wise autoregressive generator with intermediate CLIP-feature supervision and a hand-designed conditioning schedule. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish these ingredients from straightforward applications of hierarchical feature distillation and multiscale conditioning.

The central ablations are incomplete. The encoder comparison changes intermediate supervision along with the learned representation, while the guidance experiment only compares the proposed ordering with its inversion. Important controls—such as conditioning every scale on the terminal feature, using all hierarchical features at every scale, random layer-to-scale assignments, and isolating each loss—are missing.

Evaluation comparability is unclear. The paper uses an updated 1,000-image NSD test set but does not state whether every baseline was rerun on exactly that split, with identical preprocessing and candidate-selection procedures, or whether published numbers were copied. This ambiguity directly affects the claimed state of the art.

The 4.67× speed claim lacks hardware, precision, batch size, sampling settings, and whether the reported time includes encoding and selection among four generated candidates. Consequently, the wall-clock comparison is not reproducible or demonstrably fair.

The claim of deterministic and stable reconstruction conflicts with generating four candidates and selecting the best by CLIP similarity. The source of sampling variation and the reference used for candidate selection are not specified; if similarity uses the ground-truth stimulus, this would constitute test-time oracle information. Stability is supported only by one qualitative example and no quantitative diversity analysis.

Claims of superior structural faithfulness are overstated. Without the auxiliary low-level feature, low-level results remain mixed, and MindEye2 has substantially higher PixCorr and SSIM. The auxiliary feature itself is not adequately described, making the strongest low-level variant difficult to assess or reproduce.

The brain-grounding experiment is qualitative and uses known ground-truth COCO object labels. Showing selected boxes over the original stimuli without localization metrics or baseline comparisons provides little evidence for the claimed spatial faithfulness.

Several technical and reproducibility details are unclear or inconsistent: caption selection is unspecified, model dimensions and parameter counts are absent, per-subject training is not clearly described, cross-attention and AdaLN conditioning descriptions do not fully agree, and Algorithm 1 mistakenly uses the terminal feature inside the per-layer MSE loop. The stated “SoftCLIP” equation also appears to be ordinary one-directional InfoNCE rather than a soft-target CLIP objective.

The cognitive and neuroscientific interpretation is stronger than the evidence. The cortical visualization lacks quantitative region-wise statistics, uncertainty, controls, and a clear description of how feature-to-voxel regression weights yield the displayed importance maps. It does not establish that the computational hierarchy mirrors human coarse-to-fine perception.

Most diagnostics use only Subject 1, reported improvements have no uncertainty or significance testing, qualitative samples may be selectively chosen, and the complete executable code is deferred until acceptance. Overall, the promising empirical signal is not yet supported by sufficiently controlled and reproducible evidence for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive direction: replacing diffusion with scale-wise autoregression and conditioning successive scales on different fMRI-derived representations.
The reported semantic metrics are promising, particularly the CLIP, Inception, and SwAV results, and the nominal inference-time improvement could be practically valuable.
The evaluation includes multiple reconstruction metrics, per-subject results, qualitative comparisons, and initial ablations of feature supervision, CLIP-layer selection, and guidance ordering.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the coarse-to-fine formulation is easy to understand.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the main contribution. The single-feature and hierarchical-feature variants change representation and supervision together, while the guidance ablation only compares the proposed ordering against an inverted ordering. Essential controls—such as hierarchical features with fixed guidance, one feature repeated across scales, and scale-aware guidance with non-hierarchical features—are missing.

The claimed deterministic and stable reconstruction is contradicted by the appendix, which states that four candidates are generated and the best is selected using CLIP similarity. The sampling and selection procedures, source of stochasticity, selection target, and whether the reported 2.64-second runtime includes all four candidates are not specified. Stability is supported only by one qualitative example.

The strongest low-level results depend on an auxiliary low-level feature that is neither defined nor described in the method or implementation details. Consequently, a major row of Table 1 is not reproducible or technically assessable.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently established. It is unclear whether all methods were rerun on the stated updated test set under identical preprocessing and candidate-selection rules. Runtime comparisons omit hardware, batch size, sampling settings, and measurement protocol, making the 4.67× claim difficult to interpret.

The biological and cognitive claims are substantially overstated. Cascaded transformer layers supervised by CLIP layers do not by themselves demonstrate a hierarchy in the fMRI signal or correspondence to human coarse-to-fine perception. The supplementary brain analysis appears circular because representations derived from fMRI are used to predict those same fMRI voxels; it provides no clear held-out protocol, statistical analysis, or comparable color scale.

Several central empirical claims exceed the evidence. The method without auxiliary features has weak pixel-level scores, improvements over the strongest semantic baselines are often modest and lack significance testing, and the qualitative study contains only a few selected examples with no human evaluation or systematic grounding accuracy.

Reproducibility is poor: the fMRI encoder input/tokenization and tensor shapes, feature projections, loss weighting, decoding and sampling settings, caption source, per-subject training procedure, and uncertainty definition are missing. The pseudocode also contains indexing and variable errors and does not faithfully implement the stated layer mapping.

The metric description appears incorrect or ambiguous, referring to similarity between an original image embedding and a paired fMRI embedding rather than clearly defining reconstruction-based two-way identification. The reported ± values are also unexplained and do not match the visible across-subject variation.

No substantive discussion addresses privacy, consent, or misuse risks associated with reconstructing perceived images from brain activity. Overall, the idea is plausible, but the current evidence and reporting are not sufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: MindHier offers a clear and relevant contribution: it adapts scale-wise autoregressive generation to fMRI-to-image reconstruction and conditions different generation scales on different levels of an fMRI feature hierarchy. The resulting coarse-to-fine formulation is intuitive and technically plausible.

The evaluation covers strong recent baselines, eight standard low- and high-level reconstruction metrics, qualitative comparisons, per-subject results, and several targeted ablations. The full hierarchical supervision produces substantial gains over the single-feature and final-supervision variants.

The method achieves particularly strong semantic performance, including the best reported CLIP, Inception, and SwAV results without the auxiliary low-level feature. Results are reasonably consistent across the four evaluated subjects.

The reported 2.64-second inference time is a practically meaningful improvement over the listed diffusion baselines. The approach also provides natural intermediate reconstructions and potentially useful control points at different spatial scales.
The paper is generally well organized, motivates its design clearly, and provides helpful diagrams and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The inference protocol is insufficiently specified and creates a potentially serious fairness issue. The appendix says that four candidates are reconstructed and the best is selected using CLIP similarity, but it does not state what reference embedding is used, whether baseline timings and metrics use equivalent candidate selection, or whether the reported 2.64 seconds includes all four candidates. Ground-truth-dependent selection would invalidate the main comparison.

The claim that MindHier is deterministic conflicts with both autoregressive sampling and the use of four generated candidates. Figure 4 also shows non-identical outputs across trials. Consistency is demonstrated only through a few qualitative examples, without variance metrics or controlled comparisons using matched sampling settings.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Without the auxiliary low-level feature, MindHier is not best on PixCorr or SSIM; with it, some AlexNet scores remain below competing methods. Thus, claims of state-of-the-art structural faithfulness should be narrowed. Likewise, the cognitive and neuroscientific alignment claims are suggestive but not established by the reconstruction results.

The neuroscience analysis is limited and largely qualitative. It lacks statistical testing, subject-wise reporting, comparison against non-hierarchical or randomly initialized encoders, and controls showing that the apparent cortical gradient is specifically caused by the proposed hierarchy.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: model dimensions, parameter counts, loss weights, sampling parameters, random seeds, hardware, timing methodology, and several preprocessing and candidate-ranking details are missing. The pseudocode also contains indexing and variable errors, while the complete code is only promised after acceptance.

The grounding experiment uses known ground-truth COCO object labels and presents only selected qualitative cases, so it does not independently establish semantic or spatial decoding accuracy. A quantitative localization evaluation and a protocol without oracle labels would be more convincing.

The central novelty is moderate: much of the system combines hierarchical CLIP supervision with an existing pretrained scale-wise autoregressive generator. Ablations support the combination, but comparisons against simpler parameter-matched multi-layer conditioning schemes would better isolate the contribution.
